title: Personal Project Presentation Tips for MYP Year 5
summary: Personal Project presentation tips for MYP Year 5: plan your explanation, select evidence, practise questions, and understand current IB assessment guidance.
body_markdown:
A strong Personal Project presentation explains what you wanted to learn, what you created, which decisions mattered, and how you judged the result. For MYP Year 5 students, the most useful preparation is choosing evidence that makes those ideas easy to follow.


First, separate your school’s presentation event from the IB assessment requirements. The[IB’s current Personal Project overview](https://www.ibo.org/programmes/middle-years-programme/assessment-and-exams/personal-project/) identifies three connected elements: the process, the product or outcome, and the report. The report is assessed by your supervisor and externally moderated by the IB. Check with your supervisor whether your presentation is an exhibition, a school requirement, or part of an approved report format.


Imagine a student preparing to present a homemade plant-watering device. This hypothetical example will help us follow the choices involved, from selecting evidence to answering questions.


### Start with the presentation brief


Before opening your slide software, confirm:


- Who will attend: classmates, teachers, families, or visitors?
- How long will you speak, and is there separate question time?
- Are slides, a display board, a demonstration, or another format expected?
- What equipment and internet access will be available?
- How does the event relate to your assessed report?


Do not assume a slide count or speaking time applies across every IB school. Follow your school’s instructions. RevisionDojo’s[introduction to the MYP Personal Project](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-is-the-myp-personal-project) can help you place this stage within the wider project.


Our student discovers that visitors will circulate between tables. That changes the preparation: a short explanation, a working model, and a few carefully chosen images will serve the audience better than a long slide deck.


### Build your Personal Project presentation around learning


The current assessment criteria are **Planning, Applying skills, and Reflecting** . They provide a useful framework for explaining your work, although your school may specify a different presentation structure. See RevisionDojo’s[guide to the Personal Project criteria](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/myp-personal-project-criteria) for a fuller breakdown.


### Explain the learning goal and the product


These are connected but distinct. For our hypothetical student:


- **Learning goal:** understand how soil moisture sensors can control a simple watering system.
- **Product:** a device that waters a potted plant under defined conditions.


The opening should make both clear. Explain the personal interest behind the goal, then show the audience what you made.


A possible opening is: “I wanted to understand how a sensor could help care for a plant. I built this device to test whether it could respond consistently when the soil became dry.”


That gives visitors a reason to care and a question to follow.


### Select decisions that reveal your thinking


Avoid recounting every week. Choose two or three moments when research, testing, or feedback changed your approach.


For example, the student might show how an early sensor position produced inconsistent readings, then explain why they moved it. The audience sees a problem, a decision, and a consequence.


This is also where approaches to learning, or ATL, skills become concrete. Instead of saying “I used research skills,” explain how you compared sources, checked their relevance, and used the findings to make a decision. Address skills used to achieve your learning goal as well as those used to create the product.


### Choose evidence that earns its place


A finished product shows what exists now. Process evidence helps explain how it developed.


Useful choices include an annotated prototype photograph, a short testing record, a design revision, or feedback that led to a specific change. RevisionDojo’s[process journal guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/myp-personal-project-process-journal) can help you find these moments in your records.


For each item, prepare three sentences: what it shows, why it mattered, and what you did next.


Our student might place two photographs beside a small test table. The photographs show the changed sensor position; the table helps visitors understand the reason. Use your actual records, and acknowledge gaps rather than inventing measurements.


A student explains an unexpected umbrella on a homemade watering device to a visitor.


### Evaluate the outcome with specific examples


A convincing presentation includes limitations. They help the audience understand the quality of your judgment.


Return to the product success criteria you developed. Explain which were met, which were partly met, and what evidence supports your conclusion. If a criterion was too vague to evaluate reliably, acknowledge that weakness.


For the watering device, “It worked well” gives little information. A more useful explanation would describe the conditions tested, the observed performance, and any unresolved problem. Only claim what your evidence supports.


Then explain the impact on your learning. Perhaps you learned to troubleshoot circuits systematically, or discovered that interpreting a sensor reading required more investigation than assembling the device. Be precise about what changed in your understanding.


RevisionDojo’s[Personal Project report structure guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/myp-personal-project-report-structure-explained) can help you connect this explanation with your report while keeping each appropriate to its audience.


### Design for someone encountering your project for the first time


Give each slide or display section one clear purpose. Use readable text, label unfamiliar parts, and place evidence beside the explanation it supports. Credit sources for borrowed images, information, and ideas according to your school’s guidance.


For a physical product, decide how visitors can examine it safely. If a live demonstration could fail, prepare photographs or a short recording as backup. Explain honestly what any recording shows.


Our student should also define “soil moisture sensor” before discussing technical details. Familiarity can hide the very information a visitor needs first.


### Rehearse the explanation and the questions


Practise aloud with your actual materials and a timer. Ask someone unfamiliar with the project to explain back what you wanted to learn and how you evaluated the outcome. Their confusion identifies places to clarify.


Prepare for questions such as:


- Why did you choose this goal?
- Which decision made the biggest difference?
- What evidence supports your evaluation?
- What would you test or change next?


Pause before answering. Point to evidence when it helps, and say when something falls outside your investigation. RevisionDojo’s[guide to common Personal Project mistakes](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/common-myp-personal-project-mistakes-e0513f75) offers another useful preparation check.


The presentation becomes easier when your evidence carries part of the explanation. RevisionDojo can support that preparation as a central IB resource, helping you revisit the criteria, organize your thinking, and identify what still needs clarification. Aim to leave visitors understanding both the product on the table and the learning behind it.
